## Learning goals

- I can change one main test condition at a time.
- I can repeat a test and keep the raw results.
- I can explain what a benchmark does and does not measure.

## Choose a useful question

A benchmark is a repeatable task used to compare performance. Ask a focused question such as:

- Does a RAM upgrade change the time needed for the same task?
- How does a graphics setting affect frame rate?
- Does the computer slow down as it becomes warmer?

Choose a result you can measure: time, frame rate, numerical throughput, memory use, or a validated temperature reading.

## Make the test fair

- Use the same computer, software version, task, and test length.
- Change one main condition.
- Run each condition more than once.
- Record settings before the test.
- Keep the raw results.
- Stop if the computer behaves abnormally.

CPU percentage is not electrical power. Record watts only when the computer exposes a documented power sensor or the teacher supplies an enclosed wall-power meter.

## Record the results

| Condition | Trial | Result | Temperature, if available | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Baseline | 1 |  |  |  |
| Changed condition | 1 |  |  |  |

Graph the results if a graph makes the comparison easier to see. Explain variation, limits, and anything that made the test less fair.

## Check your work

Another student should be able to repeat your test from your notes. Your conclusion must match the evidence you collected.
